Two small things from writing Go-style concurrency in Scheme, and one rename.

### `(nil-channel)`

A **closed** channel is always ready in `select` — a receive takes whatever is
buffered and then the zero value — so a clause that reads one wins immediately
and for ever.  Go's answer is to assign a nil channel to the variable, and
there was no way to spell that here:

```scheme
(set! ch (nil-channel))          ; Go's ch = nil
```

A nil channel is never ready: sends and receives block for ever and `select`
never picks it, while `chan-open?` still reports that it is not closed.  That
distinction is the whole point, and it is spelled out in the README, the
channel page and the guide.  Closing one raises an ordinary condition instead
of a Go panic, and `(nil-channel?)` tells the two kinds of channel apart.

### `(continue)`

Go's `continue`, for `do` loops: inside a body it abandons the rest of the body
and goes on with the step expressions, which still run.

```scheme
(define kept '())
(do ((i 0 (+ i 1))) ((= i 5) (reverse kept))
  (if (odd? i) (continue))
  (set! kept (cons i kept)))     ; => (0 2 4)
```

It is implemented as a raise of a private condition that the loop's own guard
recognises, so it is dynamic rather than lexical — a procedure the body calls
may use it — an intervening `guard` that catches everything can intercept it,
and using it outside a loop is an ordinary catchable condition.  The guard
compares with the `eq?` primitive itself rather than the name, so a body that
rebinds `eq?` cannot break the loop.

Writing the tests for it turned up a bug of my own: the generated guard clause
was built with the wrong constructor, which flattened the clause list and made
a real error inside a `do` body disappear silently.  Fixed, with an assertion
that such an error still propagates.

### `chan-open?`

The operations on a channel are `chan-`something — `chan-send!`, `chan-recv!`,
`chan-close!` — so `channel-open?` was the odd one out and is now
**`chan-open?`**.  The old name stays as the same binding, deprecated, until
3.0.0: `(eq? chan-open? channel-open?)` is `#t`.

### Also

The release you are reading was built and published by CI: pushing a `v*` tag
now runs the five-platform test matrix and then builds the six static binaries,
runs one of them, and attaches them here.  Nothing is built or uploaded by
hand, and no cross toolchain is involved — the platforms are exercised on their
own runners rather than under qemu or wine.

2611 assertions in total: 1227 R7RS, 244 regression, 83 concurrency, 42
network, 35 process, 86 data, 43 match, 462 fast, and the SRFI suites.
